strings.title: Powers and Exponents
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: An exponent counts how many times the base is multiplied by itself: 2^5 is five 2s multiplied. Each power is the one before times the base.
strings.keywords: base, exponent, power, repeated multiplication, squared, cubed
watchFor: Multiplying base and exponent (2^3 = 6): ask "What does the 3 tell us to do with the 2?"
Adding instead of multiplying (3^3 = 9): ask "Three 3s added, or multiplied?"
Starting over every time: ask "How does 2^4 help with 2^5?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did each answer help with the next?" Land: the exponent counts the factors. Each new power is the last one times the base, so 2^5 = 2^4 × 2. Powers grow fast.

problems.notes: Look for: 2 × 2 × 2. Ask: "What does the little 3 mean?" Word choice: "2 to the power of 3", "2 cubed". Model: text 2^3 = 2 x 2 x 2 ; = 8

responses.tip: Multiplied base and exponent. Ask: how many 2s are multiplied?

problems.notes: Look for: 2^3 × 2. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: text 2^4 = 2^3 x 2 ; = 8 x 2 = 16

responses.tip: Each power is the last one times the base.

problems.notes: Look for: 16 × 2. Ask: "What's the pattern?" Model: text 2, 4, 8, 16, 32

responses.tip: Splitting the factors. Ask: why does that work?
Ask: list the 2s. How many are there?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 × 3, a square. Ask: "Why do we say 3 squared?" Model: array 3 x 3

responses.tip: Ask: draw a square with side 3. How many little squares?

problems.notes: Look for: 3^2 × 3 = 9 × 3. Ask: "Why do we say 3 cubed?" Model: text 3^3 = 3^2 x 3 ; = 9 x 3 = 27

responses.tip: Added. Ask: is an exponent repeated adding or repeated multiplying?

problems.notes: Look for: four 10s multiplied, a 1 with four zeros. Ask: "What do you notice about powers of 10?" Model: text 10^4 = 10 x 10 x 10 x 10 ; = 10 000
Look for: 2^5 × 2^5 = 32 × 32, or keep doubling. Ask: "Which earlier answer helps?" Model: text 2^10 = 2^5 x 2^5 ; = 32 x 32 = 1024

strings.title: Same Number, Different Powers
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: The same number can be written as different powers: 64 = 8^2 = 4^3 = 2^6. Regrouping the repeated factors shows why.
strings.keywords: base, exponent, power, repeated multiplication, squared, cubed, regroup factors
watchFor: Multiplying base and exponent (4^3 = 12): ask "How many 4s are multiplied?"
Thinking a bigger exponent always means a bigger number: ask "Is 2^6 bigger than 8^2?"
Not seeing the regrouping: ask "Can you group six 2s into pairs? Into threes?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why are 8^2, 4^3 and 2^6 all 64?" Land: they are the same factors grouped differently: six 2s grouped in pairs is three 4s, grouped in threes is two 8s.

problems.notes: Look for: 8 × 8. Ask: "Hold on to this." Word choice: "8 squared". Model: array 8 x 8
Look for: 4 × 4 × 4 = 16 × 4. Ask: "What do you notice?" Word choice: "4 cubed". Model: text 4^3 = 4 x 4 x 4 ; = 16 x 4 = 64
Look for: double 6 times: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. Ask: "Why is it 64 again?" Model: text 2^6 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 ; = (2 x 2) x (2 x 2) x (2 x 2) = 4^3

responses.tip: Regrouping the factors. Ask: what about groups of three 2s?

problems.notes: Look for: 9 × 9. Ask: "Is 81 another power too?" Model: area 10-1 x 9
Look for: 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 9 × 9. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: text 3^4 = (3 x 3) x (3 x 3) ; = 9 x 9 = 81

responses.tip: One 3 short. Ask: how many 3s does the 4 tell you?

problems.notes: Look for: 10 × 10 × 10. Ask: "Is 1000 a square too?" Model: text 10^3 = 10 x 10 x 10 ; = 1000

responses.tip: Ask: how many zeros should 10 × 10 × 10 have?

problems.notes: Look for: 25 × 5. Ask: "What is 5^2? Then one more 5?" Model: text 5^3 = 5^2 x 5 ; = 25 x 5 = 125
